name: OneTab
tagline: One click collapses every open tab into a list — free, no account

pricing.notes: Entirely free: no paid tier, no limits, no account required. The announced end-to-end-encrypted cross-device sync is 'coming soon' with no pricing stated, so whether sync stays free is unknown.

pros: Completely free with no account, no limits, and no upsell — rare in this category
One-click tab collapse that the developer says cuts browser memory use by up to 95%
Strong privacy stance: tab URLs are never transmitted to the developers or anyone else unless you deliberately share a list
Actively developed again — a 2026 v2 rewrite added folders, search, stars, tasks, and dark mode
Share-as-web-page turns any tab list into an instant public URL for another person or device
Plain-text export and a 2M+ Chrome install base mean lock-in is close to zero
cons: No sync yet — your list lives in one browser profile, and the promised encrypted sync is still 'coming soon'
Real data-loss risk: uninstalling the extension deletes your stored tabs, and clearing browser data can wipe them too
Saves URLs and titles only — no page content, snapshots, or full-text search, so a dead link means the content is gone
No mobile story at all: no iOS or Android app and no web app to view your list from a phone
The Mac-only Safari app is a minimal port stuck well behind the Chrome version
bestFor: Anyone drowning in open tabs who wants a free, private, zero-setup way to park them — and doesn't need sync, mobile access, or saved page content.
verdict: The best free tab parker ever made; just don't mistake a local URL list for a permanent library.
overview: OneTab is a free browser extension from UK-based OneTab Ltd that collapses every open tab into a single list with one click, cutting browser memory use by up to 95% by the developer's estimate. Tabs restore individually or all at once, and any list can be shared as a hosted web page. First released in 2013, it spent years nearly unchanged before a full v2 rewrite in 2026 added folders, in-list search, stars and tasks, and dark mode, with end-to-end-encrypted sync announced as coming soon. It stores only URLs and titles, locally in the browser profile — nothing is transmitted to the developers — and there is no account to create. Extensions exist for Chrome, Edge, and Firefox, plus a Mac-only Safari app that lags well behind. Export is a plain-text URL list. The whole product is free, with more than two million Chrome users, no limits, and no paid tier.

faqs.a: Yes, completely. OneTab has no paid tier, no limits, and doesn't even require an account — you install the extension and it works. The developer has announced encrypted cross-device sync as 'coming soon' without stating whether it will cost anything, but the core tab-collapsing product has been free since 2013 and remains so today.

Yes — and more actively than its reputation suggests. After years of near-silence that earned it an 'abandoned' label, OneTab shipped a full v2 rewrite in 2026 with folders, search, stars, tasks, and dark mode; the Chrome and Firefox extensions were both updated in July 2026. The weak spot is the Mac Safari app, which hasn't been updated since late 2024.

faqs.q: What is the best OneTab alternative?
faqs.a: For richer tab management, Workona adds synced project workspaces and Toby adds visual, shareable collections — both with free tiers. If the tabs you're parking are really things you mean to read or reference later, a bookmark manager fits better: Marqly saves all open tabs in one click, then auto-tags them and makes them findable by semantic search, which a plain URL list can't do.

No. There's no iOS app — the App Store listing is a Mac-only Safari app — no Android app, and no web app to log into, since OneTab has no accounts. Your tab list lives inside one desktop browser profile. The only way to see a list on a phone is to share it as a web page first and open that URL.

faqs.q: Can I export my data from OneTab?
faqs.a: Yes, easily. OneTab exports your saved tabs as a plain-text list of URLs with page titles, one per line, which you can copy anywhere and re-import into OneTab on another machine. You can also share any list as a hosted web page. There's no HTML, JSON, or CSV format, but a text list of URLs is about as portable as data gets.
